name: Wrist Lock
summary: The Wrist Lock (mão de vaca) is a joint lock that forces the opponent's hand into hyperflexion against the inner forearm, attacking the small wrist joint to force a fast tap; it is most accessible from closed guard top against an opponent's posting, planted hands.
description: Finish the Wrist Lock (mão de vaca) from closed guard top: flexion mechanics on planted hands, finishing steps, and defense. Success: 30/45/60%.
overview: The Wrist Lock, known in Portuguese as mão de vaca ('cow's hand') and in judo as a tekubi joint lock, is one of the most accessible and universally legal joint locks in Brazilian Jiu-Jitsu, available to every belt from white up under IBJJF rules. The standard flexion version forces the opponent's hand toward the inside of their own forearm — bending the palm down toward the wrist crease — until the small carpal joint reaches its end range and the opponent taps. From closed guard with you on the bottom, the lock is most often hunted against a posturing opponent who plants a hand on your chest, hip, or the mat to control your guard; that planted, straight-armed hand is exactly the lever the wrist lock attacks. By pinning the opponent's palm flat against your sternum or a controlled surface and then curling their fingers and palm toward their forearm, you load the wrist with very little movement and almost no telegraphing. The wrist lock is prized precisely because it punishes good posture and strong grips: the harder an opponent posts and pushes, the straighter their wrist becomes and the shorter the path to the finish. It chains naturally with collar grips, the Kimura and Americana families, and overhook control, and it serves both as a primary finish and as a way to break grips and open a stubborn defender's hands.

injury_risks.injury: Wrist sprain or ligament tear from hyperflexion
Carpal joint or scaphoid injury from sudden force
injury_risks.recovery_time: 6-12 weeks, longer if a fracture occurs

injury_risks.injury: Finger or hand strain from gripping resistance

safety_considerations.application_speed: SLOW and progressive - the wrist has a very short range before injury, so apply over 2-3 seconds and stop the instant resistance ends
tap_signals: Physical hand or arm tap with the free hand
The trapped hand going limp or stopping its resistance
Any wince or sharp distress signal as the wrist reaches end range
release_protocol: Release the flexion pressure on the wrist immediately and completely
Let the opponent's hand and forearm return to a neutral straight position
Do not jerk the hand back open — allow it to relax naturally
Check the partner's wrist and hand for any sign of injury
Confirm the partner can move the wrist through normal range before continuing
training_restrictions: Never apply the wrist lock with a jerk or snap — the joint has almost no margin
Always apply slowly and progressively, releasing the moment the partner taps
Never crank past the tap; small-joint locks injure with very little extra force

variations_and_setups.variation_name: Wrist Lock on Planted Hand (Closed Guard)
variations_and_setups.description: Against an opponent who posts a straight, planted hand on your chest or hip to posture inside closed guard, trap their palm flat with both of your hands and curl it toward their forearm. Their own posting pressure pre-loads the wrist, shortening the finish.
variations_and_setups.when_to_use: When the opponent postures up with a stiff arm and plants a hand on your torso or the mat to control distance

variations_and_setups.variation_name: Wrist Lock off the Collar Grip
variations_and_setups.description: When you hold a cross-collar or lapel grip and the opponent grips your sleeve or wrist, fold their gripping hand back over its own wrist while keeping their elbow pinned, attacking the wrist instead of fighting the grip directly.
variations_and_setups.when_to_use: In the gi when an opponent establishes a strong defensive grip on your sleeve or collar that you want to break or finish

variations_and_setups.description: When an opponent defends a Kimura or Americana by gripping their own belt, gi, or your body, fold their now-bent wrist into flexion using your figure-four frame, converting the shoulder attack into a wrist finish.
variations_and_setups.when_to_use: When a Kimura or Americana stalls because the opponent has buried their hand in a defensive grip you can fold

attacker.name: Wrist Lock Attacker
attacker.description: Finish the Wrist Lock (mão de vaca) from closed guard: trap the planted hand, fold the palm into flexion against the forearm, and finish safely with minimal motion.
attacker.overview: As the attacker, your job is to recognize a straight, planted, or gripping hand and convert it into a wrist lock with as little movement as possible. The wrist lock is a flexion attack: you bend the opponent's palm down toward the inside of their own forearm until the carpal joint reaches its end range. The single most important detail is that you must control the elbow line so the opponent cannot relieve the lock by bending their arm or rotating their shoulder. Pin their palm flat against a solid surface — most often your own sternum or the mat — then drive their fingertips toward their wrist crease while keeping their forearm from following. Because the wrist has almost no range, success is about precision and stability rather than power, and a posturing opponent who is pushing hard into you is actually feeding their own wrist into the lock.
key_principles: The wrist lock is flexion: bend the opponent's palm toward the inside of their forearm, not away from it
Trap the palm flat against a solid base — your sternum, hip, or the mat — so it cannot escape the pressure
Control the elbow line; if the elbow can travel, the opponent escapes by bending the arm and the lock dies
Use minimal motion and your whole body, not just your hands, to fold the wrist
A posting, stiff-armed opponent pre-loads their own wrist — let their pressure shorten your finish
Keep the opponent's fingers and palm together; a splayed hand can sometimes slip the angle
Apply slowly and progressively because the joint has almost no margin before injury
setup_requirements: The opponent has a straight, planted, or gripping hand within reach on your chest, hip, the mat, or your gi
You can pin or cup the opponent's palm against a solid surface with at least one of your hands
Their elbow line is controlled or about to be controlled so the arm cannot simply bend away
Your torso and hips are positioned to add body weight or rotation behind the fold
Enough head and posture control that the opponent cannot posture out before you load the wrist

execution_steps.action: Identify the planted or gripping hand
execution_steps.description: Spot the opponent's straight posting hand on your chest, hip, or the mat, or a defensive grip on your sleeve or collar, which is the lever the wrist lock attacks.
execution_steps.timing: The moment the opponent commits weight to a stiff or gripping hand

execution_steps.action: Pin the palm flat to a base
execution_steps.description: Cup or clamp the opponent's hand and press the palm flat against a solid surface such as your sternum or the mat so the hand cannot retract while you load the joint.
Trap or frame against the opponent's elbow so their arm cannot bend or rotate to follow the wrist, ensuring all the pressure stays in the wrist joint rather than dissipating into the arm.
execution_steps.timing: As you pin the palm, before adding flexion

execution_steps.description: Drive the opponent's fingertips and palm down toward the inside of their forearm, folding the wrist into flexion while the forearm stays pinned in place.
execution_steps.timing: Once the palm and elbow are controlled

execution_steps.description: Use your chest, hips, or a slight rotation of your torso to drive the fold rather than relying on hand strength alone, keeping the motion small and controlled.
execution_steps.timing: As the wrist begins to load

execution_steps.action: Close the angle to end range
execution_steps.description: Continue the flexion smoothly until the opponent's wrist reaches its end range, keeping the elbow trapped so they cannot relieve the pressure by straightening or rotating.

execution_steps.action: Finish and release on the tap
execution_steps.description: Apply the final increment of flexion over a couple of seconds and release the instant the opponent taps, allowing their hand to return to neutral without snapping it back.
execution_steps.timing: Final phase, always with safety priority

common_counters.counter: Opponent bends their elbow and pulls the hand back before you load the wrist
common_counters.your_response: Stay attached to the hand and re-pin it, or release the wrist and retain your closed guard if the arm escapes the angle.

common_counters.counter: Opponent straightens and rotates the wrist out of flexion alignment
common_counters.your_response: Re-establish the palm pin against your sternum and trap the elbow before re-applying the fold so the joint cannot rotate free.

common_counters.counter: Opponent drives forward, postures, and starts to stack or pass as you reach for the hand
common_counters.your_response: Abandon the wrist if your guard is compromised, re-frame and recover, rather than chasing the finish into a passed guard.

common_counters.counter: Opponent splays the fingers and grips your gi to disperse the pressure
common_counters.your_response: Gather their fingers and palm together, re-seat the flat pin, and reapply flexion with the hand as a single unit.

common_errors.error: Bending the wrist in extension instead of flexion
common_errors.consequence: You attack the wrong direction, the opponent simply resists, and the lock generates no real pressure
common_errors.correction: Fold the palm toward the inside of the forearm; the standard mão de vaca is a flexion lock, not extension

common_errors.error: Letting the opponent's elbow travel or bend
common_errors.consequence: The arm follows the wrist, the pressure dissipates into the shoulder and elbow, and the finish disappears
common_errors.correction: Trap or frame the elbow line first so every degree of fold loads the wrist joint itself

common_errors.error: Relying on hand and finger strength alone
common_errors.consequence: A strong opponent out-muscles your grip, you fatigue, and the wrist never reaches end range
common_errors.correction: Pin the palm to a solid base and drive the fold with chest, hips, or torso rotation instead of just your hands

common_errors.error: Failing to pin the palm flat
common_errors.consequence: The hand retracts or slides off your body and the joint never loads, letting the opponent escape easily
common_errors.correction: Clamp the palm flat against your sternum, hip, or the mat so it cannot retract while you fold the wrist

common_errors.consequence: The small wrist joint has almost no margin and a snap risks a serious sprain or fracture even on a tapping partner
common_errors.correction: Apply slowly over two to three seconds and release instantly on the tap to keep training safe

training_progressions.description: Drill identifying a posting or gripping hand from closed guard and naming the flexion direction, without applying pressure, to build the trigger reflex.
Practice pinning the partner's palm flat to your sternum and trapping the elbow line, holding the controlled position without finishing to ingrain the structure.
Apply gradual flexion with a cooperative partner who taps early, building feel for the very short range and the immediate release timing.
Spar from closed guard hunting the wrist lock against a posturing partner, finishing or abandoning under progressive resistance while respecting tap signals.

flashcards.question: In which direction do you bend the wrist to finish the standard wrist lock (mão de vaca)?
flashcards.answer: You bend it in flexion — folding the opponent's palm and fingers down toward the inside of their own forearm until the carpal joint reaches end range. The standard mão de vaca is a flexion lock, not an extension lock.

flashcards.question: Why is a posturing opponent who plants a stiff hand on your chest vulnerable to the wrist lock?
flashcards.answer: A straight, posting arm pre-loads the wrist: the harder they push, the straighter the joint becomes and the shorter the path to flexion. You pin that planted palm flat and fold it toward their forearm with minimal motion.

flashcards.question: What must you control besides the hand for the wrist lock to work?
flashcards.answer: You must control the elbow line. If the opponent can bend their arm or rotate the shoulder, the forearm follows the wrist and the pressure dissipates. Trapping the elbow keeps every degree of fold loading the wrist joint.

flashcards.question: Why should you pin the opponent's palm to a solid base before applying the lock?
flashcards.answer: Pinning the palm flat against your sternum, hip, or the mat stops the hand from retracting and gives you a stable platform to fold against, so your body weight rather than finger strength loads the wrist.

flashcards.question: How do you generate finishing pressure on the wrist without out-muscling a strong opponent?
flashcards.answer: Drive the fold with your chest, hips, or a small torso rotation against a pinned palm, using whole-body mechanics. The motion stays small; the wrist has very little range, so precision and a stable base matter more than raw strength.

flashcards.question: How can a defended Kimura or Americana be converted into a wrist lock?
flashcards.answer: When the opponent buries their hand in a defensive grip on their belt, gi, or your body, their wrist is already bent. Using your figure-four frame, you fold that bent wrist further into flexion, turning the shoulder attack into a wrist finish.

flashcards.question: What is the most common error that makes a wrist lock fail entirely?
flashcards.answer: Bending the wrist in the wrong direction or letting the elbow travel. The mão de vaca must be a flexion fold with the elbow trapped; attacking extension or letting the arm bend dissipates all the pressure.

flashcards.question: Why must the wrist lock be applied slowly, and when do you release?
flashcards.answer: The wrist and carpal joints have almost no margin before a sprain or fracture, so a snap can injure even a tapping partner. Apply over two to three seconds and release the instant the partner taps, goes limp, or signals distress.

flashcards.question: Your closed-guard opponent postures and plants both hands to open your guard — how do you turn that into an attack?
flashcards.answer: Trap one planted palm flat against your chest, control that elbow line, and fold the hand toward their forearm into flexion. Their posting pressure shortens the finish, and even a failed attempt can break their posture and grip.

flashcards.question: If your wrist lock fails from closed guard, what is the safe fallback?
flashcards.answer: Retain your closed guard rather than chasing the finish into a passed position. If the opponent escapes the hand and starts to stack or pass, abandon the wrist, re-frame, and recover your guard to stay safe.

defender.name: Wrist Lock Defender
defender.description: Defend the Wrist Lock (mão de vaca): recognize the flexion attack on a posting hand, free the wrist by bending the elbow, and tap early to protect the small joint.
defender.overview: As the defender, you are usually the top player posturing inside closed guard with a planted hand that has just been isolated. The wrist lock attacks your hand by folding it into flexion against your own forearm, so your defense centers on never leaving a stiff, straight, exposed hand for the opponent to trap. The single most important escape principle is that the wrist lock dies when the elbow bends: if you can bend your arm and bring your elbow toward your own body, your forearm follows your hand and the joint unloads. Recognition has to be early because the wrist has almost no range — by the time you feel sharp pain, you are already at the finish. Keep your hands moving and your fingers active rather than posting stiffly, retract a trapped hand by bending the elbow, and if the lock is sealed and your hand is genuinely pinned, tap early. No grip, posture, or position is worth a wrist injury from a joint with so little margin.
key_principles: The wrist lock dies when the elbow bends — pulling your elbow toward your body unloads the joint
Never leave a stiff, straight, planted hand exposed for the opponent to pin and fold
Recognize the flexion attack early; the wrist has almost no range before injury
Keep your hands and fingers active and moving rather than posting rigidly
Free the trapped hand by retracting the whole arm, not by fighting just the wrist
If your hand is genuinely pinned and the fold is sealed, tap early rather than risk the joint
Avoid feeding posting pressure into a hand the opponent has already begun to trap
recognition_cues: The opponent traps and pins your posting or gripping hand flat against their chest or the mat
You feel your palm being folded down toward the inside of your own forearm
Your elbow is being framed or trapped so your arm cannot bend away
Sharp, localized pressure building in the wrist rather than the elbow or shoulder

defensive_options.action: Bend the elbow and retract the trapped hand before the wrist loads
defensive_options.when_to_use: The instant you feel the opponent pin your palm and begin folding it
defensive_options.if_successful: You free the wrist, keep your hand, and stay in top position inside the guard
defensive_options.risk: Reacting late lets the fold reach end range before the elbow can travel

defensive_options.action: Posture, drive forward, and start to stack or pass to take the angle away
defensive_options.when_to_use: When your guard-passing position is strong and you can pressure forward off the trapped hand
defensive_options.if_successful: You break the opponent's attacking frame and continue toward passing the guard
defensive_options.risk: Driving into a deep wrist lock can accelerate the finish if the hand is already sealed

defensive_options.action: Open the hand, splay the fingers, and grip to disrupt the flat pin
defensive_options.when_to_use: When the palm pin is not yet fully seated and you can change the hand's shape
defensive_options.if_successful: You disperse the pressure and prevent the wrist from folding as a single unit
defensive_options.risk: If the opponent re-gathers the fingers and re-seats the pin, the lock returns

escape_paths: Bend the elbow and pull the whole arm back to recover a free, mobile hand
Posture and drive forward to pass and remove the opponent's attacking angle
Tap early and reset if the wrist is genuinely sealed at end range

favorable_outcomes.how: Recognize the wrist attack early, posture and drive your weight forward off the trapped hand to break the opponent's attacking frame, and continue working to open and pass the closed guard.
Bend your elbow and retract the trapped hand before the fold loads, freeing the wrist while the opponent keeps closed guard, so you reset the exchange without conceding the finish.

common_errors.error: Leaving a stiff, straight, planted hand on the opponent for too long
common_errors.consequence: You hand the attacker a ready-made lever, and your own posting pressure pre-loads the wrist for the fold
common_errors.correction: Keep your hands active and moving, and avoid posting rigidly with a straight, exposed arm inside the guard

common_errors.error: Fighting the wrist instead of bending the elbow
common_errors.consequence: You try to muscle the wrist straight while the elbow stays extended, and the joint stays loaded and reaches end range
common_errors.correction: Bend the elbow and retract the whole arm so the forearm follows the hand and the wrist unloads

common_errors.error: Ignoring the lock until it hurts
common_errors.consequence: The wrist has almost no range, so by the time you feel sharp pain you are already at the finish with no time to react
common_errors.correction: Recognize the palm pin and folding cue early, and either escape immediately or tap before the joint is injured

flashcards.question: What is the single most reliable way to escape a wrist lock once your hand is trapped?
flashcards.answer: Bend your elbow and retract the whole arm toward your body. The wrist lock dies when the elbow bends, because your forearm then follows your hand and the joint unloads instead of reaching end range.

flashcards.question: Why is leaving a straight, planted hand on a closed-guard opponent dangerous?
flashcards.answer: A stiff, posting hand is the exact lever the wrist lock attacks. Your own pushing pressure pre-loads the wrist, so the opponent only has to pin the palm and fold it toward your forearm to reach the finish quickly.

flashcards.question: Why must you recognize the wrist lock early rather than waiting to feel pain?
flashcards.answer: The wrist and carpal joints have almost no range before injury, so by the time you feel sharp pain you are essentially at the finish. Early recognition of the palm pin and fold is what gives you time to escape.

flashcards.question: How can changing the shape of your hand disrupt a developing wrist lock?
flashcards.answer: Splaying your fingers and gripping disperses the flat palm pin, so the wrist cannot fold as a single rigid unit. Breaking up that pin buys time to bend the elbow and retract the arm before the lock develops.

plausible: Make a tight fist and keep the arm straight so the attacker has nothing loose to bend against.
Go completely limp through the hand and wrist so there is no structure for the attacker to torque.
trap: Yank the arm straight back as hard as you can to rip the pinned hand out of the attacker's grip.

flashcards.question: If your hand is genuinely pinned and the wrist is folded to end range, what should you do?
flashcards.answer: Tap early — no grip, posture, or position is worth a wrist sprain or fracture from a joint with so little margin. Tap with the free hand, foot, or voice, and reset rather than fighting a sealed lock.

plausible: Stay calm and slowly peel the attacker's fingers open one by one before the pressure fully peaks.
Turn your body toward the fold to relieve the angle, tapping only if the pressure keeps building.
trap: Spin explosively toward the locked wrist to unwind the fold before the attacker can finish.

training_progressions.description: Drill from closed guard top recognizing when a cooperative partner pins your posting hand and begins folding it, practicing the early-warning read before any real pressure is applied.
Practice bending the elbow and retracting the whole arm the instant the palm is pinned, building the reflex to unload the wrist by moving the arm rather than fighting the joint.
Spar from closed guard top against a partner hunting the wrist lock, choosing in real time whether to retract, posture and pass, or tap, while respecting safety on the small joint.
